title: Resilience buffering and burst-cost proposal for dedicated GPU pools
content:
Purpose:
This is a working proposal for a resilience-oriented buffering approach to dedicated GPU pools. Focus: reduce customer-visible throttling during bursty demand while keeping committed GPU costs constrained. Document is intended for the customer POC workshop on Jan 26 and for Solutions Eng to use when sizing Dedicated proposals that allow short bursts above committed capacity.

Context and motivation:
- Customers often have spiky traffic (cron-driven imports, launch events) that cause short-lived 10–20x bursts over baseline. Committing full capacity for peaks is expensive.
- Existing autoscale reacts but cold starts and allocation time for new GPU instances mean brief queuing and increased tail latency.
- We want a proposal combining: a small committed pool, a warm buffer (prewarmed but limited), and a burst credit model backed by low-latency allocation fallback. This doc quantifies tradeoffs and provides cost heuristics.

High-level design (three layers):
1) Committed pool (C): baseline capacity sized for expected day-to-day throughput and steady-state SLOs. This is fully reserved and provides predictable latency/cost.
2) Warm buffer (W): a small number of prewarmed GPU slots (hot instances, pinned processes) kept ready to accept new requests within target tail latency. Costed as partially committed (higher cost than pure burst but far cheaper than fully provisioning for peaks). W is typically 10–30% of peak.
3) Elastic burst (B): ephemeral instances that can be spun up on demand or pulled from cloud burst capacity. Accepts degraded SLO (higher tail latency) and best-effort fallbacks; used for infrequent large spikes.

Sizing heuristics and formulas (working):
Inputs we ask from customer:
- baseline RPS (requests/sec) average and 95th percentile over 30 days
- typical request type (generation vs embeddings) and average tokens-out
- SLOs: median latency target and 95th/99th tail latency targets
- acceptable percent of requests that can see degraded performance during bursts (e.g., 0.5% of monthly tokens)

Throughput model assumptions (example):
- Model: 30B decoder-only family (serving profile similar to small-llama models).
- H100 throughput: 120 tokens/sec sustained per GPU at seq_len=256 for batching-friendly workloads.
- A10G throughput: 28 tokens/sec per GPU at seq_len=256.
- Average tokens per request (payload+response): 120 tokens.
- Concurrency model: continuous batching reduces per-token cost; assume effective concurrency = 20 requests per GPU for generation workloads.

Sizing example (customer A, guidance):
- Baseline avg RPS: 25 req/s, P95 RPS: 40 req/s
- Tokens per req: 120 tokens -> tokens/s at P95 = 40 * 120 = 4800 tokens/s
- If using H100 (120 tokens/s/gpu): required GPUs at P95 = ceil(4800 / 120) = 40 GPUs (committed) -> this is expensive.
- Alternative: commit for baseline (avg) + warm buffer + burst:
  - Commit for avg: avg tokens/s = 25 * 120 = 3000 tokens/s -> 3000/120 = 25 GPUs (C=25)
  - Warm buffer W = 10% of (peak - committed) -> (40-25) * 0.1 = 1.5 ~ 2 GPUs
  - Elastic burst B handles remainder of peaks (40 - 25 - 2 = 13 GPUs), only active during spikes.

Cost model (placeholder hourly rates used for proposals):
- H100 dedicated hour price (internal cost assumption): $18.00 / GPU-hour
- A10G equivalent: $4.50 / GPU-hour
- Warm buffer is priced as reserved for billing but expected utilization is low; in proposals we amortize buffer cost into committed price (no special line item).

Monthly cost example (approx):
- Commit C=25 H100 GPU-hours -> 25 * 24 * 30 * $18 = $324,000/month
- Warm buffer W=2 -> 2 * 24 * 30 * $18 = $25,920/month (we roll this into C in many offers)
- Burst B usage: assume 6 peak hours/month at 13 GPUs -> 13 * 6 * $18 = $1,404/month
- Total raw infra = $351k/month (note: large portion is baseline commitment). This shows the economics: burst hours are tiny relative to commit.

Tradeoffs and customer-facing options (pricing constructs):
Option A (strict commit): commit for P95 (40 GPUs). Pros: simplest, predictable. Cons: heavy cost during normal, poor unit economics.
Option B (buffered commit - recommended): commit for avg + small warm buffer + cheap burst credits for rare peaks. Pros: lowers base cost, keeps short tails healthy. Cons: requires SLA language for degraded performance during scaling and clear burst quotas.
Option C (hybrid with spot/cheaper GPUs): commit smaller on H100, allow burst to A10G for less critical paths (risky for latency/quality mismatches).

Autoscale policy proposal (practical rules):
- Scale-up triggers:
  - If queued requests > threshold (queue > 50 across pool) OR token throughput > 80% of capacity for 30s -> allocate W (if available) then B as next step.
  - B allocations are prioritized by customer tier and by predicted remaining spike duration (if < 5 minutes, B only; if > 10m, consider larger allocation).
- Scale-down rules:
  - Cooldown 10m after any scale-up before scale down.
  - Gradual drain: mark instances for drain and stop accepting new work, wait for running requests to finish (max drain window 3m) then deallocate.
- Prewarm policy:
  - During known events (deploys, marketing pushes), prewarm additional W slots 30m before expected start.
- Guardrails:
  - Max burst usage per day (GPU-hours) tied to customer burst credit balance. Alerts at 50%, 80%, 100%.

Operational considerations and optimizations:
- Prefix/KV caching: ensure ephemeral bursts can reuse KV caches where possible to reduce warmup penalty; keep small persistent cache nodes that can serve cache lookups even if model instances are warming.
- Canary policy: new model variants should be routed to committed pool first; burst nodes run stable variants only.
- Auto-fallback: when B cannot allocate, fallback to degraded model (quantized variant) that runs on smaller GPU types with explanatory response headers.

Workshop outcomes and decisions (summary):
- Customer agrees to pilot Option B for 60 days with the following targets: P95 latency < 500ms for committed pool; tail degradation allowed up to 2s for bursts (<=1% of monthly tokens).
- Initial commit set to C=10 H100 GPUs based on customer-provided avg RPS (note: this is lower than the worked example above; scaled to their numbers).
- Warm buffer W set to 2 GPUs; burst credit allocation of 200 GPU-hours/month.

Open questions / action items:
- Priya to validate H100 per-GPU throughput numbers for the exact model the customer will run (action: PRF-78).
- Marco to draft SLA language for burst credit exhaustion and fallback behavior by Jan 30.
- Evan to instrument a short synthetic spike test to measure real-world cold start (action: runbook spike-01).
- Need legal signoff on pricing construct for warm buffer amortization (finance ticket FIN-893).

Notes to self (raw):
- Watch out for mixing GPUs across pools: KV cache incompatibility can increase cold-latency substantially.
- Consider offering a measured "burst insurance" addon: small monthly fee that converts burst hours above threshold to higher-priority allocation. Could be an upsell.
- When proposing to customer, show 3-month cost-sensitivity chart: commit sizes vs expected peak hours and estimated monthly cost.

Appendix: quick sensitivity sketch (text):
- If average tokens increase by 25% -> committed GPUs needed increase roughly same ratio; buffer becomes more valuable.
- If burst frequency > 10 events/month, then Option B loses advantage; consider bumping commit or negotiating higher burst credits.

End of working draft.

-- Aisha
